nodes.title: B. Applicability of Regulations under SBR Framework
nodes.summary: The directions set a 24‑month compliance window for newly classified NBFC‑ULs, allow phased business growth, and require a Board‑approved roadmap to be sent to RBI. NBFC‑ULs must remain under enhanced regulation for a minimum of five years, unless they voluntarily restructure (but not for financial distress). Criteria for classification are reviewed regularly, with the asset‑size threshold reviewed every three years. Lower‑layer rules automatically cascade upward, with specific provisions for NBFC‑BL, ML, UL and TL—TLs face higher capital charges and intensified supervision. Group NBFCs of scheduled commercial banks must follow commercial‑banking directions where applicable, yet keep their scale‑based classification. Registration is mandatory for companies whose principal business meets the asset and income tests. NBFCs not using public funds, lacking customer interfaces, and with assets below ₹1,000 cr become exempt from registration and can deregister by end‑2026.

nodes.title: Chapter-III – Registration requirement
nodes.summary: The section outlines the comprehensive requirements for NBFC registration, covering criteria, principal business definition, and specific exemptions for entities not using public funds or lacking a customer interface. It details deregistration procedures, documentation, and group aggregation rules, along with auditor reporting mandates. The distinction between Type I and Type II registrations, overseas investment restrictions for unregistered Type I NBFCs, and Net Owned Fund thresholds and glide‑paths for various NBFC categories are specified, along with the NOF calculation rules that deduct group exposures and AIF investments. FATF‑non‑compliant jurisdiction investment limits and beneficial ownership rules are imposed, restricting new investors to under 20% voting power and setting a 50% trust threshold, while existing investors may retain stakes. Finally, exemptions under RBI Act 1934 for certain NBFC categories are enumerated with their specific conditions.

nodes.title: A. Principal Business Criteria
nodes.summary: The document details NBFC registration criteria, defines principal business, explains exemption for NBFCs not availing public funds or having customer interface, outlines deregistration procedures and required documentation, sets aggregation rules for groups, mandates auditor reporting, distinguishes Type I and Type II registration obligations, restricts overseas investment for unregistered Type I NBFCs, clarifies that exemptions only cover sections 45IA and 45IC, and specifies Net Owned Fund requirements with a glide path for existing NBFC‑ICC, NBFC‑MFI, and NBFC‑Factor to meet the ₹10 crore threshold.

nodes.title: B. Net Owned Fund Requirement
nodes.summary: The document details that unregistered Type I NBFCs are exempt only from sections 45IA and 45IC but remain under other RBI provisions and can be instructed or penalised by the RBI; FAQs on exemptions are referenced. It sets NOF thresholds of ₹10 crore for NBFC‑ICC/MFI/Factor, ₹2 crore for NBFC‑P2P/AA/Type I, and ₹300 crore for NBFC‑IFC/IDF‑NBFC, provides a glide‑path for existing NBFCs to reach ₹10 crore by 2025/2027, and states that failure to meet these levels bars registration. Specific NOF and registration rules for various NBFC categories are listed per RBI directions. For NOF calculation, any investment, loan or exposure to subsidiaries, same‑group companies or other NBFCs that exceeds 10% of paid‑up equity capital and free reserves is subtracted, including investments made through AIFs in company form. The amendment effective 01 July 2026 is also noted.

nodes.title: C. Investment through Alternative Investment Funds - Calculation of NOF of an NBFC
nodes.summary: The text outlines NOF thresholds and eligibility for NBFC registration, specifies category‑specific NOF and registration rules per RBI directions, explains NOF calculation including deductions for group exposures, treats AIF investments with >50% NBFC contribution as equivalent to direct holdings, restricts new investments from FATF non‑compliant jurisdictions to under 20% of voting power, defines FATF compliance, and allows pre‑existing investors to retain their stakes.

nodes.title: D. Investment from FATF non-compliant jurisdictions
nodes.summary: The text outlines regulatory rules for NBFC investments, defining beneficial ownership in trusts (50% threshold) and emphasizing substance over form. It restricts new investors from FATF non‑compliant jurisdictions to less than 20% of an NBFC’s voting power, including potential voting rights, while allowing existing investors to continue. It then lists specific exemptions from RBI Act 1934 for NBFCs that operate payment systems, issue prepaid instruments, provide microfinance loans under RBI directions, are securitisation or reconstruction companies, or are Nidhi companies, detailing conditions such as asset size, licensing, and deposit acceptance.

nodes.title: Chapter-IV - Exemptions from the provisions of the RBI Act, 1934
nodes.summary: Chapter‑IV of the RBI Act, 1934 grants broad exemptions to a wide range of non‑banking institutions from Chapter III B, sections 45‑IA, 45‑IB, 45‑IC, 45‑MB, 45‑MC and related RBI directions, conditioned on regulatory registration, asset limits, non‑acceptance of public deposits and other specific criteria. The exempted entities include payment‑system operators, micro‑finance NBFCs, securitisation and reconstruction firms, Nidhi and mutual‑benefit companies, chit firms, merchant banks, mortgage‑guarantee firms, housing‑finance units, insurers, stock exchanges, stock brokers/sub‑brokers, alternative investment funds, core investment companies and special NBFCs. All exemptions take effect from 1 July 2026 as per the RBI amendment directions.

nodes.title: A. Exemption from provisions of Chapter III B of the RBI Act, 1934 to the following:
nodes.summary: Chapter-IV of the RBI Act 1934 exempts certain non‑banking institutions from specified provisions. Exemptions include: (i) NBIs authorized to run payment systems and issue prepaid payment instruments under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007, but only for the money received for those instruments; (ii) non‑banking financial companies that provide only micro‑finance loans, meet income‑based loan limits, are licensed under Companies Act 1956/2013, do not accept public deposits, and have assets below ₹100 crore; (iii) securitisation and reconstruction companies registered under the 2002 Securitisation Act; and (iv) Nidhi companies notified under section 620A of the Companies Act. These entities are exempt from Chapter III B and sections 45‑IA, 45‑IB, 45‑IC of the RBI Act.

nodes.title: B. Exemption from sections 45-IA, 45-IB and 45-IC of the RBI Act, 1934 to the following:
nodes.summary: The Reserve Bank exempts a range of non‑banking financial institutions—including payment‑system operators, microfinance NBFCs, securitisation and reconstruction entities, Nidhi and mutual benefit companies, chit firms, merchant banks, mortgage guarantee firms, housing finance units, insurers, stock exchanges, brokers, and alternative investment funds—from various provisions of the RBI Act, specifically sections 45‑IA, 45‑IB, 45‑IC, 45‑MB, 45‑MC, and Chapter III B, provided they meet specified conditions (such as limits on loan obligations, asset size, deposit acceptance, and regulatory registration). These entities are further exempt from the RBI Directions on acceptance of public deposits (except Chapter IV) and other listed directions.

nodes.title: C. Exemption from sections 45-IA, 45-IB, 45-IC, 45-MB and 45-MC of the RBI Act, 1934 to the following:
nodes.summary: The text specifies that certain non‑banking financial companies—insurance firms, stock exchanges, stock brokers/sub‑brokers, and alternative investment funds—are exempt from specific sections of the RBI Act (45‑IA, 45‑IB, 45‑IC, 45‑MB, 45‑MC) provided they hold the required registration certificates, do not accept public deposits as defined in RBI Directions 2025, and are exempt from the Directions (except Chapter‑IV) and the directions referred to in paragraph 5.

nodes.title: D. Exemption from sections 45-IA and 45-IC of the RBI Act, 1934 to the following:
nodes.summary: The text enumerates various exemptions from RBI Act sections 45‑IA, 45‑IB, 45‑IC, 45‑MB, and 45‑MC for specific categories of non‑banking financial companies: insurance companies, stock exchanges, stock brokers/sub‑brokers, alternative investment fund companies, a special type of NBFC that neither takes public funds nor serves customers, unregistered core investment companies, and core investment companies meeting capital and leverage norms. These entities also enjoy exemptions from the RBI Directions on NBFCs accepting public deposits (excluding Chapter‑IV and paragraph 5 of those Directions). The exemptions become operative from July 1, 2026 per the RBI amendment directions of April 29, 2026.

nodes.title: E. Exemption from section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934 to the following:
nodes.summary: The text outlines conditions for NBFCs that do not use public funds or have customer interfaces, specifies exemptions from section 45‑IA of the RBI Act for both unregistered and registered core investment companies meeting capital and leverage criteria, and notes that these provisions take effect from July 1 2026 under the RBI amendment directions.

nodes.title: F. Exemption from section 45-IA(1)(b) of the RBI Act, 1934 to the following:
nodes.summary: The text sets out detailed exemption criteria for NBFCs that neither use public funds nor have customer interfaces, requiring asset limits, board resolutions, and disclosure of their status; it grants section 45‑IA exemptions for both unregistered and registered Core Investment Companies, subject to capital and leverage standards; these rules took effect on 1 July 2026 as per RBI amendment, and all NBFCs must follow the reporting requirements set by the RBI Department of Supervision.

nodes.title: Chapter-V – Reporting Requirements
nodes.summary: The document mandates that all NBFCs adhere to the Reserve Bank's reporting requirements; it repeals previous directions on registration, exemptions, and scale‑based regulation, while preserving the legal effect of actions, approvals, and penalties that were governed by those repealed directions; it also clarifies that these new directions coexist with, not replace, other existing laws and regulations.

nodes.title: Chapter-VI – Repeal and Other Provisions
nodes.summary: The RBI has repealed all existing directions on registration, exemptions, and scale‑based regulation of NBFCs as of 28 November 2025. Actions taken under the old rules remain governed by them and the repeal does not affect rights, obligations, penalties, or legal proceedings. The new directions supplement other laws and RBI may issue binding clarifications.

nodes.title: Chapter II – Grant of No Objection Certificate (NOC) / Approval by RBI
nodes.summary: The text outlines RBI approval requirements for voluntary amalgamations involving NBFCs. All such amalgamations must first secure RBI NOC or prior approval before any Court or Tribunal action. Specific conditions trigger prior approval: changes in control, a 26% or higher shareholding shift, or more than 30% director change. nodes.title: Chapter I- Preliminary
nodes.summary: The Reserve Bank of India issues Directions on 2025 governing acquisition of shareholding or control of various NBFCs. They specify the short title, effective date, applicability to listed NBFC categories, and exclusions. Definitions for key terms are provided. The Directions mandate prior RBI written permission for any takeover or control acquisition of an NBFC, for shareholding increases of 26% or more of paid‑up equity (except court‑approved buybacks), and for foreign investor increases of 10% or more in HFCs that accept public deposits (except court‑approved buybacks). nodes.summary: The RBI has instituted a comprehensive prior‑approval regime for NBFCs and HFCs acquiring significant shareholding or control, requiring PRAVAAH applications with detailed shareholder information, source of funds, declarations and a bankers’ report, plus a 30‑day public notice in national and local newspapers (with certain exemptions). Shareholding changes in SPDs also need approval and reporting. Investments from FATF non‑compliant jurisdictions face stricter limits, capping new investors’ voting power at 20% (including potential voting rights), while existing investors may retain their positions. Actions taken under repealed directives remain governed by those directives, and RBI may provide clarifications.

nodes.title: C. Requirement of prior Public Notice about Change in Control/ Management
nodes.summary: The text outlines RBI procedures for NBFCs: they must file a prior approval application via PRAVAAH with detailed shareholder disclosures and a bankers’ report; before any ownership or control change, a public notice must be published in national and local newspapers, except for certain HFC shareholding changes by foreign investors; the notice must be issued with RBI permission. Additionally, investments from FATF non‑compliant jurisdictions are treated as less favourable; new investors from such jurisdictions cannot hold significant influence and must stay below 20 % of voting power (including potential voting rights), while existing investors before classification may continue as per existing rules.

nodes.summary: {"points":["Public notice must state intention to sell or transfer ownership/control, details of transferee, and reasons for sale/transfer.","Investments in NBFCs from FATF non‑compliant jurisdictions are not treated on par with those from FATF compliant jurisdictions.","A jurisdiction is FATF compliant if it is not listed in the FATF High‑Risk or Increased Monitoring lists.","New investors from or through non‑compliant FATF jurisdictions cannot acquire significant influence; they must hold less than 20% of the NBFC’s voting power, including potential voting power.","Potential voting power includes convertible instruments, contingent voting rights, or contractual arrangements that could grant future voting rights.","Existing investors who held investments before a jurisdiction was classified non‑compliant may continue and add investments under existing regulations.","Existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines relating to acquisition of shareholding/control in NBFCs are repealed.","Actions taken under the repealed directives remain governed by those directives; rights, obligations, penalties, investigations and remedies continue as if not repealed.","The provisions of these Directions are in addition to, not contrary to, other laws, rules, regulations, or directions in force.","The RBI may issue clarifications to facilitate application or interpretation of these Directions."]}

nodes.title: Chapter III- Repeal and Other Provisions
nodes.summary: The document repeals all prior directions on shareholding/control acquisition for NBFCs, ensuring that actions taken under those directives remain governed by them and that rights, liabilities, penalties, and legal proceedings are unaffected; the directions supplement existing laws. The RBI may issue clarifications whose interpretations are final and binding. Annex I provides Form 1(a), a mandatory information sheet for proposed promoters/shareholders, detailing personal, contact, identification, educational, professional, regulatory, prosecutorial, default, disciplinary, and disqualification information.

RBI Branch Authorization Directions for NBFCs 2025
nodes.summary: The RBI, exercising its statutory authority, issues the Reserve Bank of India (Non‑Banking Financial Companies – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025, effective immediately. These directions apply to all layers of specified NBFCs (NBFC‑D, NBFC‑ICC, NBFC‑Factor, NBFC‑MFI, NBFC‑IFC, IDF‑NBFC, and HFCs) under certain provisions. The directions were amended on 15 April 2026 with new amendments.

nodes.title: B. Applicability
nodes.summary: The Reserve Bank of India issued the “Non‑Banking Financial Companies – Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025” which come into force immediately. They apply to all layers of NBFCs registered under the RBI Act 1934 and related acts, specifically including NBFC‑D, NBFC‑ICC, NBFC‑Factor, NBFC‑MFI, NBFC‑IFC, IDF‑NBFC, and housing finance companies under the NHB Act 1987. Paragraphs 5, 10‑11, and 13‑15 govern these entities; paragraphs 6 and 12 apply to deposit‑taking NBFCs and deposit‑taking housing finance companies; paragraphs 10, 13‑15 also apply to CICs. Certain entities—Mortgage Guarantee Companies, Special Purpose Companies, P2P NBFCs, Asset‑backed NBFCs, and NOFHCs—are excluded. The directions are amended as of 15 April 2026. Applicability follows the framework set out in the 2025 NBFC Registration, Exemptions and Scale‑Based Regulation Directions. All terms are defined as per the Banking Regulation Act 1949, RBI Act 1934, or the RBI glossary.

nodes.title: Note: The applicability under these Directions is in line with the regulatory structure for NBFCs as set out in Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2025.
nodes.summary: The document specifies that certain regulatory paragraphs apply to deposit‑taking NBFCs and HFCs under RBI and NHB Acts, and to CICs, while explicitly excluding MGCs, SPDs, NBFC‑P2P, NBFC‑AA, and NOFHCs from these directions. It aligns with the RBI’s 2025 NBFC regulatory framework and reaffirms that undefined terms retain their meanings from relevant statutes and RBI glossaries.

nodes.title: C. Definitions
nodes.summary: The Directions set rules for deposit‑taking NBFCs, HFCs, and CICs, specifying applicability, exclusions, and alignment with 2025 regulatory frameworks. Definitions default to standard RBI and banking statutes. NBFCs can open branches without RBI approval unless restricted, with location limits based on NOF and credit rating. Specific paragraphs have been deleted or amended effective 15 April 2026.

nodes.title: NBFC Branch Authorization Guidelines and Amendments
nodes.summary: The page outlines NBFC branch authorization rules, stating that NBFCs generally need no RBI approval to open branches unless restricted. Deposit‑taking NBFCs under RBI Directions 2025 may open branches or appoint agents based on NOF and credit rating: limited to their state if NOF ≤ ₹50 cr or rating below AA; nationwide if NOF > ₹50 cr and rating AA or higher. An NBFC with NOF > ₹50 cr but rating below AA is limited to its state. Sections A2 and A3 are deleted, and amendment directions effective 15 April 2026 replace prior rules and delete specified items.

nodes.summary: The text outlines that NBFCs can open domestic branches without RBI approval, except under specific restrictions, and specifies conditions based on NOF and credit rating for branch expansion. Deposit‑taking NBFCs must notify RBI and the public before closing branches, with a required three‑month notice period. NBFCs may not generally open foreign branches; those already abroad must have notified RBI and follow 2025 Directions. Opening representative offices abroad requires prior RBI approval via PRAVAAH portal, limited to liaison activities, with no fund outlay or credit lines, and must obey host‑country regulations.

nodes.title: NBFC Branch Operations: Opening, Closure, and Representative Offices Abroad
nodes.summary: The document outlines that NBFCs cannot open new foreign branches but may continue existing ones under 2025 regulations; closing any branch requires a three‑month newspaper notice and a subsequent RBI notification for deposit‑taking NBFCs; opening a foreign representative office needs RBI approval through the PRAVAAH portal, is restricted to liaison and research activities without fund outlay, and all provisions are updated by April 15 2026.

nodes.title: C.    Opening of representative offices abroad
nodes.summary: The directions state that NBFCs (except CIC & HFC) cannot open new foreign branches, though existing ones may continue under RBI 2025 rules. Branch closures require a three‑month public notice in a national and local vernacular newspaper, with deposit‑taking NBFCs sending a copy to the RBI within seven days. Opening a representative office abroad requires RBI approval via the PRAVAAH portal and is limited to liaison, market study or research with no fund outlay or credit lines; host‑country regulations apply and periodic reports must be submitted, otherwise approvals may be recalled. The directions were amended on 15 April 2026. All earlier NBFC branch‑authorisation directives are repealed, but actions, approvals, and penalties under them remain governed by their provisions and are unaffected by the repeal. The new directions supplement existing laws, and RBI may issue further clarifications.

nodes.title: Repeal of Branch Authorization Directives and Related Provisions
nodes.summary: The document repeals all prior NBFI branch authorization directives, maintains the validity of actions and approvals taken under them, ensures that rights, obligations, penalties, and legal processes are unaffected by the repeal, adds the new directions on top of existing laws, and allows RBI to issue further orders for clarity.

nodes.title: C. Interpretations
nodes.summary: The new Directions repeal prior NBFC branch‑authorization guidelines, preserving earlier repeals and ensuring that existing actions, approvals, and legal matters remain governed by the repealed rules. They add to current laws without conflict, and the RBI can issue binding clarifications.
